rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The companion forgot to tell Moses what he had witnessed about the fish, rather than forgetting the fish itself; the phrase about remembering is a grammatical substitute for the forgotten report.
rows.anchor: أي نسيت حال الحوت التي شاهدتها منه فلم أذكرها لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the companion was Joshua, attributing the lapse to Satan poses no problem: prophetic protection bars sinful influence, not every non-sinful harm.
rows.anchor: والأنبياء في عصمة إلهية من الشيطان لأنهم معصومون مما يرجع إلى المعصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposal that the companion says the fish took a wondrous course while Moses adds “wondrous” is rejected by the context.
rows.anchor: قول الفتى وقوله { عجبا } من قول موسى، والسياق يدفعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier possible readings of the pair’s forgetting also apply here; the fish event marks the divinely indicated meeting place, whether by its specific revival and escape or a general sign involving its loss or return to life.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن ما تقدم من الاحتمال في قوله { نسيا حوتهما } الخ جار ها هنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baghy means seeking, irtidad is returning to a starting point, athar means their footprints, and qasas is following a trace; Moses retraced their steps to the fish’s location.
rows.anchor: والقصص اتباع الأثر والمعنى قال موسى ذلك الذي وقع من أمر الحوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fish’s event was the sign of the meeting-place revealed to Moses, either as the specific event or more generally as loss, revival, or return of the dead fish.
rows.anchor: يكشف عن أن موسى كان مأمورا من طريق الوحي أن يلقى العالم في مجمع البحرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every blessing is divine mercy; outward blessings operate through ordinary causes, while inward gifts such as prophecy and divine friendship are bestowed without them.
rows.anchor: ومنها ما لا يتوسط فيه شيء منها كالنعم الباطنيه من النبوة والولاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majestic plural and angels’ role in revelation support interpreting “mercy from Us” as prophethood rather than divine friendship, which belongs exclusively to God.
rows.anchor: وكون النبوة مما للملائكة الكرام فيه عمل كالوحي ونحوه يؤيد أن يكون المراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowledge “from Our presence” is gifted rather than acquired through sense, thought, or ordinary causes, and later verses identify it as knowledge of events’ interpretation.
rows.anchor: فهو علم وهبي غير اكتسابي يختص به أولياءه وآخر الآيات يدل على أنه كان علما بتأويل الحوادث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rushd means the opposite of error and reaching what is correct; it functions either as a purpose complement or as the object taught, yielding two close readings of Moses’ request.
rows.anchor: الرشد خلاف الغي وهو إصابه الصواب، وهو في الآية مفعول له أو مفعول به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic negation, indefinite “patience” under negation, and denial of ability make Khidr’s warning stronger than simply saying Moses will not be patient.
rows.anchor: ونفي الصبر بنفي الاستطاعة التي هي القدرة فهو آكد من أن يقال لن تصبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses cannot patiently witness acts whose reality and interpretation he does not know; the obstacle is missing knowledge that would let him see why they must occur.
rows.anchor: وهو إحاطة الخبر والعلم بحقيقة الواقعة وتأويلها حتى يعلم أنها يجب أن تجري على ما جرت عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses reacts to the visible acts, not their explanations, just as he did not react when told at Sinai that his people worshipped the calf until he saw it.
rows.anchor: وقد كان الله أخبره بذلك وهو في الميقات فلم يأت بشيء من ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khubr means knowledge and is an accusative specification; the question means Moses’ knowledge does not encompass the matter.
rows.anchor: الخبر العلم وهو تمييز والمعنى لا يحيط به خبرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ promise of patience and not disobeying was qualified by God’s will, so his later impatience did not make it false; Khidr had not yet forbidden questions.
rows.anchor: وعده الصبر لكن قيده بالمشيئة فلم يكذب إذ لم يصبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Mention it” means Khidr will initiate an explanation of a troubling event; Moses should wait for that explanation instead of asking first.
rows.anchor: وإحداث الذكر من الشيء الابتداء به من غير سابقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses shows exceptional humility: he asks rather than commands, calls companionship following, and presents teaching as his own learning rather than a condition imposed on Khidr.
rows.anchor: فلم يورد طلبه منه التعليم في صورة الأمر بل في صورة الاستفهام هضما لنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses honors Khidr’s learning as knowledge from an unnamed source, praises it as guidance, asks only for a portion, and treats disobedience to Khidr as disobedience to an order.
rows.anchor: ثم أعظم قدر علمه إذ جعله منتسبا إلى مبدأ غير معلوم لم يعينه باسم أو نعت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses completes his deferential manner by expressing his promise indirectly and adding “if God wills.”
rows.anchor: ثم لم يسترسل معه بالتصريح بالوعد بل كنى عنه بمثل قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr likewise shows good manners: he hints at refusal through Moses’ inability, leaves following to Moses’ choice, and makes the no-question rule a condition of following.
rows.anchor: وقد تأدب الخضر معه إذ لم يصرح بالرد أولا بل أشار إليه بنفي استطاعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imr means a great calamity; the resultative lam describes the ship’s necessary consequence as though intended, though Khidr did not intend drowning.
rows.anchor: فإن الغرق وإن كان عاقبة للخرق ولم يقصده الخضر البتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative’s “they set out” indicates Moses did not take Joshua along on the journey with Khidr.
rows.anchor: وهو ظاهر في أن موسى لم يصحب فتاه في سيره مع الخضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr’s question rebukes Moses for objecting and recalls the earlier warning that he could not remain patient.
rows.anchor: إنكار لسؤال موسى وتذكير لما قاله من قبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahq is oppressive suffocation and irhaq is imposing a burden; Moses asks not to be held to his forgotten promise or made to bear hardship. Reading forgetting as abandonment is reported, but forgetting is preferred.
rows.anchor: وربما يفسر النسيان بمعنى الترك، والأول أظهر، والكلام اعتذار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boat exit is omitted. “He killed him” joins the conditional sequence, while “he said” answers “when,” so the passage foregrounds Moses’ objection rather than the killing.
rows.anchor: فخرجا من السفينة وانطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The syntax of the boy and wall episodes matches: the acts are part of the conditional sequence and Moses’ objection is its focus; unlike the boat episode, where damaging the ship itself answers “when.”
rows.anchor: وبذلك يظهر أن العمدة في الكلام ذكر اعتراض موسى لا ذكر القتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses tell one story of Moses’ three successive objections, not three separate stories of Khidr’s actions each followed by an objection.
rows.anchor: فالقصة قصة اعتراضاته فهي واحدة لا قصة أعمال هذا واعتراضات ذاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakiyya means pure from sins; Moses’ question objects to killing someone who appeared innocent.
rows.anchor: والمراد طهارتها من الذنوب لعدم البلوغ كما يشعر به قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some infer from “without a life” that the boy was an adult, since a minor cannot commit murder requiring retaliation.
rows.anchor: وربما استفيد من قوله { بغير نفس } أنه كان شابا بالغا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghulam can refer to an adult or a minor, so the word alone does not prove he was underage; Moses means no offense appeared to warrant death.
rows.anchor: ولا دلالة في إطلاق الغلام عليه على عدم بلوغه لأن الغلام يطلق على البالغ وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Without a life” means without a retaliatory killing that could legally justify his death; no such offense was apparent to Moses.
rows.anchor: أي بغير قتل منها لنفس قتلا مجوزا لقتلها قصاصا وقودا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nukr is what people find abhorrent; killing is more appalling than damaging a boat, which only indirectly risks lives.
rows.anchor: وهو أفظع وأفجع عند الناس من الخرق الذي يستوجب عادة هلاك النفوس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The added “to you” sharpens the rebuke: Moses ignored the warning, as if he had not heard or thought it meant someone else.
rows.anchor: نوع تقريع له أنه لم يصغ إلى وصيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “After this” refers to this occasion or objection; if Moses asks again, Khidr may end their companionship.
rows.anchor: أي إن سألتك بعد هذه المرة أو هذه المسألة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You have reached an excuse from me” means Moses has given Khidr a complete excuse to end their relationship.
rows.anchor: أي بلغت عذرا ووجدته كائنا ذلك من لدني إذ بلغ عذرك النهاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The village episode’s sequence of setting out, refusal, finding the wall, and repairing it has the same syntax as the preceding boy episode.
rows.anchor: كالكلام في قوله في الآية السابقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text names the village’s inhabitants because only they can be asked for food; unlike arrival at a village, asking for food cannot be attributed to the place itself.
rows.anchor: لرداءة قولنا قرية استطعماهم بخلاف مثل قولنا أتى قرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naming the inhabitants also shows they were present when the wall was repaired, so Moses could suggest taking wages from them; the travelers were hungry.
rows.anchor: دليل على أن إقامة الجدار كانت بحضور من أهل القرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istitaama means requesting food by association, which is why the text says the residents refused to host them.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالاستطعام طلب الطعام بالاضافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wall’s desire to collapse is figurative for being on the verge of falling; Khidr repaired it but the text does not specify how.
rows.anchor: وإراده الانقضاض مجاز عن الاشراف على السقوط والانهدام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr may have repaired it miraculously, by construction, or with a prop; Moses’ suggestion of wages favors ordinary workmanship.
rows.anchor: مشعر بأنه كان بعمل غير خارق فإن المعهود من أخذ الأجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Takhadha and akhadha share the meaning “take”; “on it” refers to repairing the wall, and the hunger context explains Moses’ suggestion of wages.
rows.anchor: والسياق يشهد أنهما كانا جائعين فذكره موسى أخذ الأجرة على عمله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative may refer to Moses’ words as the cause of separation, the moment as the time of separation, or the separation itself now arriving.
rows.anchor: ويمكن أن تكون الإشارة إلى نفس الفراق، والمعنى هذا الفراق قد حضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Between me and you,” instead of “between us,” emphasizes separation; Khidr announces it after the third objection, when Moses had already accepted it as the consequence of another question.
rows.anchor: وإنما قال الخضر هذا القول بعد الاعتراض الثالث لأن موسى كان قبل ذلك يعتذر إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about damaging the vessel shows that the king seized sound ships, so Khidr made this one defective to keep it from being taken.
rows.anchor: وقوله { أن أعيبها } أي أجعلها معيبة وهذه قرينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waraʾ can mean behind or something out of sight or threatening even when ahead; a tyrant king was taking ships by force, so damage protected their owners.
rows.anchor: ومحصل المعنى أن السفينة كانت لعدة من المساكين يعملون بها في البحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We feared” is figurative caution arising from compassion, not emotional fear, which is denied of God and His prophets.
rows.anchor: أن يكون المراد بالخشية التحذر عن رأفة ورحمة مجازا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading is that the boy would overwhelm his parents by drawing them through his influence and their love into tyranny and disbelief.
rows.anchor: أي يحمل والديه على الطغيان والكفر بالإغواء والتأثير الروحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about a child closer in kinship supports taking tyranny and disbelief as descriptions of the boy himself, rather than sins imposed on his parents.
rows.anchor: تميزين عن الإرهاق أي وصفين للغلام دون أبويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Better in zakah means greater righteousness and faith, in contrast with tyranny and disbelief; zakah originally means purity.
rows.anchor: المراد بكونه خيرا منه زكاة كونه خيرا منه صلاحا وإيمانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Closer in kinship” means more dutiful to relatives, not simply more compassionate toward his parents, which fits the wording better.
rows.anchor: وأما تفسيره بكونه أكثر رحمة بهما فلا يناسبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parents’ faith mattered to God and called for a righteous child who would maintain kinship; God commanded Khidr to kill the boy and replace him.
rows.anchor: إلى أن إيمان أبويه كان ذا قدر عند الله ويستدعي ولدا مؤمنا صالحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The city may differ from the village where the wall stood: mentioning the orphans’ location matters because neither they nor their guardians were present.
rows.anchor: فكأن العناية متعلقة بالإشارة إلى أنهما ومن يتولى أمرهما غير حاضرين في القرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The orphans, treasure, and righteous father prepare the explanation that God wanted them to mature and recover it; mercy motivates the plan, since a fallen wall would expose the treasure.
rows.anchor: فرحمته تعالى سبب لإرادة بلوغهما واستخراجهما كنزهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The father’s righteousness occasioned divine mercy protecting the orphans and their treasure after his death.
rows.anchor: وكان سبب انبعاث الرحمة صلاح أبيهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse says the treasure belonged to the orphans and does not establish that their father buried it; if he did, his righteousness and a valid purpose keep this from being blameworthy despite the warning against hoarding.
rows.anchor: لكن الآية لا تتعرض بأكثر من أن تحته كنز لهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A parent’s righteousness can pass beneficial effects and happiness to descendants, paralleling the warning about leaving vulnerable offspring.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية دلالة على أن صلاح الإنسان ربما ورث أولاده أثرا جميلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr’s statement that he did not act on his own means he acted under God’s command.
rows.anchor: عن أمر غيره وهو الله سبحانه لا عن أمر أمرته به نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Qur’anic usage, taʾwil is the underlying reality to which something returns: a dream’s interpretation, a ruling’s rationale, an act’s real purpose, or an event’s actual cause.
rows.anchor: التأويل في عرف القرآن هي الحقيقة التي يتضمنها الشيء ويؤول إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explanations give the real causes of the three acts, not Moses’ surface readings of shipwreck, unjust killing, and poor management of livelihood.
rows.anchor: هو السبب الحقيقي لها لا ما حسبه موسى من العناوين المترائية من أعماله

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some explain Khidr’s careful wording as attributing a deficient act to himself, shared agency to himself and God, and a purely providential outcome to God.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعضهم أن من الأدب الجميل الذي استعمله الخضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God directs Moses to a servant with knowledge Moses lacks and a sign at the sea meeting; Moses travels with his companion carrying a dead fish, which revives or disappears by the rock while the companion watches but forgets to report it.
rows.anchor: أوحى الله سبحانه إلى موسى أن هناك عبدا من عباده عنده من العلم ما ليس عند موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After they travel on and grow tired, Moses asks for food; the companion recounts the fish event, attributing his failure to mention it to Satan or his own forgetting, and Moses recognizes the sign and retraces their steps.
rows.anchor: قال موسى ذلك ما كنا نبغي ونطلب فلنرجع إلى هناك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They find God’s servant, granted divine mercy and gifted knowledge, and Moses asks to follow him and learn guidance God taught him.
rows.anchor: فعرض عليه موسى وسأله أن يتبعه فيعلمه شيئا ذا رشد مما علمه الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr warns that Moses cannot patiently observe acts whose interpretation he does not know; Moses promises patience if God wills, and Khidr asks him not to question until he explains.
rows.anchor: قال العالم إنك لن تستطيع معي صبرا على ما تشاهده من أعمالي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr damages a boat carrying passengers; Moses protests that it endangers them, is reminded of the warning, and apologizes for forgetting his promise.
rows.anchor: فخرق العالم السفينة خرقا لا يؤمن معه الغرق فأدهش ذلك موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr kills a boy; Moses objects, is reminded again, and, with no further excuse, asks for one more chance, agreeing that another question will end their companionship.
rows.anchor: فلم يكن عند موسى ما يعتذر به ويمتنع به عن مفارقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A village refuses the hungry travelers hospitality; Khidr repairs a threatened wall, Moses suggests wages to buy food, and Khidr separates from him before explaining the acts.
rows.anchor: وقد بلغ بهما الجوع فاستطعما أهلها فلم يضيفهما أحد منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boat belonged to poor people who made their living at sea; a king seized every sound vessel, so Khidr damaged theirs to deter him.
rows.anchor: وكان وراءهم ملك يأخذ كل سفينة غصبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boy was an unbeliever whose tyranny and disbelief would burden his believing parents; God ordered his death and replacement by a better, more dutiful child.
rows.anchor: وأما الغلام فكان كافرا وكان أبواه مؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wall protected the treasure of two orphan boys until maturity; their father’s righteousness moved God’s mercy, and Khidr acted by God’s command.
rows.anchor: فشملتهما الرحمة الإلهية لصلاح أبيهما فأمرني أن أقيمه

rows.speaker: الصادق عليه السلام
rows.claim: A report says Khidr was a commissioned prophet who called his people to God’s oneness and affirmation of the prophets, messengers, and scriptures; wherever he sat, dry wood and bare earth turned green, hence his name, and it gives his lineage.
rows.anchor: عن الصادق عليه السلام أن الخضر كان نبيا مرسلا بعثه الله تبارك وتعالى إلى قومه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas and Abu Hurayra says Khidr was named for praying on white furwa that turned green.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس وأبي هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم قال إنما سمي الخضر خضرا

rows.speaker: أحدهما عليهما السلام
rows.claim: A report transmitted by al-Ayyashi from Burayd says Khidr and Dhul-Qarnayn were learned men, not prophets.
rows.anchor: الخضر وذو القرنين كانا عالمين ولم يكونا نبيين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story’s verses appear to establish Khidr’s prophethood, since divine rulings descended on him.
rows.anchor: لكن الآيات النازلة في قصته مع موسى لا تخلو عن ظهور في كونه نبيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports from the Imams say Khidr is still alive; extraordinary longevity is within God’s power and no rational proof makes it impossible.
rows.anchor: أنه حي لم يمت بعد وليس بعزيز على الله سبحانه أن يعمر بعض عباده عمرا طويلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some public-channel reports say Khidr was Adam’s son and lived until the Antichrist, or that Adam prayed he live until the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: أنه ابن آدم لصلبه ونسئ له في أجله حتى يكذب الدجال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports from both traditions say Khidr drank from the Water of Life in darkness while accompanying Dhul-Qarnayn, who did not drink it.
rows.anchor: أنه شرب من عين الحياة التي هي في الظلمات حين دخلها ذو القرنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These and similar solitary reports cannot be verified through decisive scripture, Prophetic tradition, or reason.
rows.anchor: وهذه وأمثالها آحاد غير قطعية من الأخبار لا سبيل إلى تصحيحها

rows.speaker: خصيف
rows.claim: A fanciful report lists Jesus and Idris in heaven, Khidr at sea, and Ilyas on land among four living prophets; the author dismisses such unreliable tales.
rows.anchor: كرواية خصيف أربعة من الأنبياء أحياء اثنان في السماء عيسى وإدريس

rows.speaker: العقيلي عن كعب
rows.claim: A fanciful report places Khidr on a pulpit between the seas, with sea creatures obeying him and spirits presented morning and evening; the author says such tales are not credible.
rows.anchor: ورواية العقيلي عن كعب قال الخضر على منبر بين البحر الأعلى والبحر الأسفل

rows.speaker: كعب الأحبار
rows.claim: A tale says Khidr dived in the Indian or Chinese Sea and an angel said a man since David had not reached one-third of its depth after three hundred years; the author dismisses such tales.
rows.anchor: ورواية كعب الأحبار أن الخضر بن عاميل ركب في نفر من أصحابه

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد عليه السلام
rows.claim: In a long report, Moses’ miracles and learning lead him to think no one is more knowledgeable; God sends Gabriel to direct him to a worshipper at the sea meeting, and Moses travels with Joshua to find Khidr.
rows.anchor: فأوحى الله إلى جبرئيل أدرك عبدي قبل أن يهلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Burhan, al-Ayyashi, and al-Qummi transmit the story through several routes; al-Durr al-Manthur records many routes from Ibn Abbas, Ubayy b. Kaʿb, and the Prophet in major collections.
rows.anchor: وروى القصة العياشي في تفسيره بطريقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reports agree with the story’s opening and say the fish was alive at the rock before taking a tunnel-like path through the sea, while differing in many additions.
rows.anchor: والأحاديث متفقة في معنى ما نقلناه من صدر حديث محمد بن عمارة

rows.speaker: ابن بابويه والقمي
rows.claim: Their reports locate the meeting of the seas in Syria and Palestine and identify the village as Nazareth; the author infers this from their details.
rows.anchor: أن مجمع البحرين من أرض الشامات وفلسطين بقرينة ذكرهما

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi identifies the two seas as the Kurr and Rass flowing into the sea and names the village Bajrawan, whose people were miserly.
rows.anchor: عن السدي أن البحرين هما الكر والرس حيث يصبان في البحر

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: A report attributed to Ubayy identifies the village as Africa.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أبي أنه أفريقية

rows.speaker: القرظي
rows.claim: Al-Qurazi identifies the village as Tangier.
rows.anchor: وعن القرظي أنه طنجة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada identifies the meeting of the seas as the Byzantine and Persian seas.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة أنه ملتقى بحر الروم وفارس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports vary on whether the carried fish was grilled or salted; most say it was salted.
rows.anchor: ومنها ما في بعض الروايات أن الحوت كان مشويا وفي أكثرها أنه كان مملوحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some reports place a life-giving spring at the rock whose water grants immortality and revives dead things; other versions say Joshua’s ablution drop revived the fish, or he drank without permission and Khidr put the fish in a vessel to remain until the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: حتى في رواية مسلم وغيره أن الماء كان ماء الحياة من شرب منه خلد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the spring was where Khidr drank; many other reports do not mention it.
rows.anchor: وفي بعضها أنه كانت عند الصخرة عين الحياة التي كان يشرب منها الخضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many canonical reports say the fish entered the sea through a tunnel, with God holding the current so the water arched over it; some add that Moses followed the path over water, parting it with his staff, and that the fish’s passage turned the sea to rock.
rows.anchor: فأمسك الله عن الحوت جرية الماء فصار عليه مثل الطاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most reports place Moses’ meeting with Khidr at the rock; variants put him on an island reached by the fish’s trail or sitting or reclining on the water.
rows.anchor: ومنها ما في أكثرها أن موسى لقي الخضر عند الصخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Narrations differ on whether Joshua accompanied them and on how Khidr damaged the boat, killed the boy, repaired the wall, and what the treasure contained.
rows.anchor: ومنها اختلافها في أن الفتى هل صحبهما أو تركاه وذهبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most versions make the treasure a gold tablet of maxims and identify the righteous father as the orphans’ immediate father; others place seven, ten, seventy, or seven hundred ancestors between them.
rows.anchor: لكن أكثر الروايات أنه كان لوحا من ذهب مكتوبا فيه مواعظ

rows.speaker: الرضا عليه السلام
rows.claim: A report answering which teacher was more learned and whether anyone could be Moses’ authority says Moses met Khidr on an island; Khidr said each had been assigned a task the other could not bear.
rows.anchor: قال إني وكلت بأمر لا تطيقه، ووكلت بأمر لا أطيقه الحديث

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
rows.claim: A report authenticated by al-Hakim from Ubayy says a bird dipped its beak in water; Khidr compared Moses’ and his own knowledge to what the bird took from God’s knowledge. Most story reports include it.
rows.anchor: أخرج الحاكم وصححه عن أبي أن النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم قال

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
rows.claim: A report from Hisham b. Salim says Moses knew more than Khidr; the author reconciles reports as referring to different kinds of knowledge.
rows.anchor: عن هشام بن سالم عن أبي عبد الله عليه السلام قال كان موسى أعلم من الخضر

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر عليه السلام
rows.claim: Abu Hamza reports from Abu Jaʿfar that Joshua son of Nun was Moses’ successor and the companion mentioned in the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: عن أبي حمزه عن أبي جعفر عليه السلام قال كان وصي موسى يوشع بن نون

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله عن أبيه عليهما السلام
rows.claim: A report says that when an Israelite claimed no one knew God better than Moses, God disclosed Khidr; the fish was the sign by which Moses could find him.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن ميمون القداح عن أبي عبد الله عن أبيه عليهما السلام قال

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
rows.claim: Abu Basir reports that Khidr feared the boy would call his parents to disbelief and their intense love would make them obey him.
rows.anchor: خشي إن أدرك الغلام أن يدعو أبويه إلى الكفر فيجيبانه من فرط حبهما له

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
rows.claim: One report says the parents had a girl who later bore a prophetic boy; most reports say she bore seventy prophets, with the author explaining an intermediary in the chain.
rows.anchor: قال إنه ولدت لهما جارية فولدت غلاما فكان نبيا

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
rows.claim: Ishaq b. Ammar reports that God blesses a believer’s descendants and surrounding households for the believer’s righteousness, then points to the orphans as an example.
rows.anchor: عن إسحاق بن عمار قال سمعت أبا عبد الله عليه السلام يقول أن الله ليصلح بصلاح الرجل المؤمن

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Jaʿfar and his forefathers says God preserves a righteous person’s family and property after death, even if the family is wicked, and then cites the verse about the father’s righteousness.
rows.anchor: إن الله ليخلف العبد الصالح بعد موته في أهله وماله

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Jabir says God improves the children and grandchildren of a righteous person and protects surrounding households; reports on this point are numerous and widespread.
rows.anchor: إن الله يصلح بصلاح الرجل الصالح ولده وولد ولده وأهل دويرات حوله

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
rows.claim: Safwan al-Jammal reports that the treasure was not coins but a tablet with four maxims: God’s oneness, certainty of death, reckoning, and destiny.
rows.anchor: أما إنه ما كان ذهبا ولا فضة، وإنما كان أربع كلمات لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many reports say the treasure was a written tablet, usually of gold; “not gold or silver” means not coinage, so the accounts do not conflict.
rows.anchor: لأن المراد به نفي الدينار والدرهم كما هو المتبادر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The maxims vary, but most versions agree on God’s oneness and themes of death and destiny; some combine the two testimonies and additional maxims in a report from Ali.
rows.anchor: والروايات مختلفة في تعيين الكلمات التي كانت مكتوبة على اللوح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage introduces Dhul-Qarnayn’s story and contains matters about future events.
rows.anchor: على قصة ذي القرنين، وفيها شيء من ملاحم القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They ask about Dhul-Qarnayn’s story, not his identity: the answer recounts what he did and does not even give his personal name.
rows.anchor: والدليل على ذلك جوابه عن السؤال بذكر شأنه لا تعريف شخصه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Remembrance” can mean a narrated account about Dhul-Qarnayn, or the Qur’an, which God calls remembrance elsewhere; the second reading is stronger.
rows.anchor: والمعنى الثاني أظهر. قوله تعالى { إنا مكنا له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an uses God’s saying for prophetic revelation or communication and also for inspiration to a non-prophet; thus “We said to Dhul-Qarnayn” does not prove he was a prophet.
rows.anchor: لكون قوله تعالى أعم من الوحي المختص بالنبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording about return to his Lord may suggest Dhul-Qarnayn spoke through an accompanying prophet, like Saul’s kingship under a prophet’s direction.
rows.anchor: من إشعار بأن مكالمته كانت بتوسط نبي كان معه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hasanan is either a verbal noun standing for an adjective or an intensive description; some see the pairing of kindness with punishment as favoring kindness.
rows.anchor: فحسنا مصدر بمعنى الفاعل قائم مقام موصوفه أو هو وصف للمبالغة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some read God’s statement as granting Dhul-Qarnayn a choice to punish or show kindness; the author instead reads it as asking what he intends to do, which better explains his detailed answer.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل إن في مقابلة العذاب باتخاذ الحسن إيماء إلى ترجيحه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement is an inquiry about Dhul-Qarnayn’s policy after conquering the people: he will punish wrongdoers and treat faithful, righteous people well.
rows.anchor: لكن الظاهر أنه استخبار عما سيفعله بهم من سياسة أو عفو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command omits the object of punishment because not everyone was a wrongdoer, whereas kindness could be extended to all, good and bad alike.
rows.anchor: ليس من الجائز تعميم العذاب لقوم هذا شأنهم بخلاف تعميم الإحسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nukr means unfamiliar and unexpected punishment, one the offender has neither known nor anticipated.
rows.anchor: النكر والمنكر غير المعهود أي يعذبه عذابا لا عهد له به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpret wrongdoing as polytheism and punishment as killing, by contrast with the faithful; the author prefers a broader sense including any corruption and sees no basis for restricting punishment to execution.
rows.anchor: الظلم بالإشراك. والتعذيب بالقتل فمعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The syntax treats “righteous” and “the best” as adjectives standing for nouns; reward can be parsed as a state, specification, or cognate object, yielding the reward of good conduct.
rows.anchor: وصف أقيم مقام موصوفه وكذا الحسنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yusr means something made easy; the likely meaning is that Dhul-Qarnayn will give manageable commands and not burden the believer.
rows.anchor: اليسر بمعني الميسور وصف أقيم مقام موصوفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhul-Qarnayn travels east to a desert and finds nomadic people without shelter from the sun; they lack houses, tents, and clothing because they have not learned to make them.
rows.anchor: فوجد الشمس تطلع على قوم بدويين لم نجعل لهم من دونها سترا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Thus” points back to the people’s described condition; comparing a thing to itself by alleging a difference adds emphasis, while other proposed referents are remote.
rows.anchor: وتشبيه الشيء بنفسه مبنيا على دعوى المغايرة يفيد نوعا من التأكيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s comprehensive knowledge of Dhul-Qarnayn’s resources and circumstances implies his choices and movements were guided by God, as in the western journey.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن إحاطة علمه تعالى بما عنده كناية عن كون ما اختاره وأتى به بهداية من الله وأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The guidance reading parallels God’s command to Noah, His revealing by His knowledge, and His encompassing knowledge of messengers.
rows.anchor: الخ في معناها الكنائي نظيرة قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings emphasize Dhul-Qarnayn’s greatness, journey hardships, or the magnitude of the means he used; the author judges his guidance interpretation better.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن الآية لإفادة تعظيم أمره وأنه لا يحيط بدقائقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sadd means a mountain or any barrier to passage, and “below them” means nearby.
rows.anchor: السد الجبل وكل حاجز يسد طريق العبور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their near inability to understand speech indicates simple understanding; the alternative that their language was remote from known languages is far-fetched.
rows.anchor: المعروفة عندهم، ولا يخلو عن بعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The speakers are the people near the mountains; context indicates Yajuj and Majuj were human peoples raiding them with killing, captivity, and plunder.
rows.anchor: ويأجوج ومأجوج جيلان من الناس كانوا يأتونهم من وراء الجبلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kharj is money paid for a need; the people offer payment for a barrier that stops Yajuj and Majuj from raiding them.
rows.anchor: الخرج ما يخرج من المال ليصرف في شيء من الحوائج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhul-Qarnayn declines their payment because God’s provision and power are better, but asks for labor and materials to build a stronger barrier.
rows.anchor: استغناء من ذي القرنين عن خرجهم الذي عرضوه عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Makkani derives from m-k-n-n with one nun assimilated; rدم means a barrier and may mean a stronger barrier, exceeding what they requested.
rows.anchor: ثم أدغمت إحدى النونين في الأخرى، والردم السد وقيل السد القوي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His request for strength means manpower and materials; he names iron, copper, and bellows, and their offer was effectively wages for building the barrier.
rows.anchor: أعينوني بما أتقوى به على بنائه كالرجال وما يستعمل في بنائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zubar is the plural of zubrah, a piece; sawa means level, with a variant “sawwa”; the paired ṣadafs are mountain sides, and qitr is molten copper or brass poured into gaps.
rows.anchor: الزبر بالضم فالفتح جمع زبرة كغرف وغرفة وهي القطعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iron is named as the key to the barrier’s strength; its command is either partitive apposition to the request for help or an omitted “he said.”
rows.anchor: ولعله خصها بالذكر ولم يذكر الحجارة وغيرها من لوازم البناء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text omits that the people supplied labor and materials and Dhul-Qarnayn built the barrier to the mountain sides before commanding them to blow.
rows.anchor: فاعانوه بقوة وآتوه ما طلبه منهم فبنى لهم السد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Blow” leaves its object unstated to focus on blowing; bellows heat the iron before copper is poured into the gaps.
rows.anchor: والمراد نصب المنافخ على السد لإحماء ما وضع فيه من الحديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the mass was made like fire in appearance and heat, the description uses ellipsis and metaphor.
rows.anchor: أي كالنار في هيئته وحرارته فهو من الاستعارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He pours molten copper into the holes and gaps so the barrier becomes solid and impassable.
rows.anchor: ليسد بذلك خلله ويصير السد به مصمتا لا ينفذ فيه نافذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asṭāʿū and istaṭāʿū mean the same; the barrier’s height prevents Yajuj and Majuj from climbing, and its strength prevents boring through.
rows.anchor: اسطاع واستطاع واحد، والظهور العلو والاستعلاء، والنقب الثقب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dakkāʾ means crushing and is a verbal noun used for the passive result; another view compares it to a flat camel, a metaphor for destruction.
rows.anchor: الدكاء الدك وهو أشد الدق مصدر بمعنى اسم المفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhul-Qarnayn calls the barrier mercy from God because it protects peoples from Yajuj and Majuj.
rows.anchor: أي السد رحمة من ربي أي نعمة ووقايه يدفع به شر يأجوج ومأجوج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise may be a specific end-times prophecy about this barrier, or the general promise of the Resurrection when mountains and the world are destroyed; God’s promise is certain.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالوعد إما وعد منه تعالى خاص بالسد أنه سيندك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronouns refer to humanity generally; surging against one another depicts people rushing chaotically like waves at the day’s terror, with order collapsing and divine care withdrawn.
rows.anchor: والمراد أنهم يضطربون يومئذ من شدة الهول اضطراب البحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The depiction of humanity surging together elaborates Dhul-Qarnayn’s concise statement that the barrier will be crushed when God’s promise arrives.
rows.anchor: فالآية بمنزلة التفصيل للإجمال الذي في قول ذي القرنين
